bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Regulatory, permitting and land-acquisition delays — The Indian infrastructure sector, particularly highway, bridge and flyover construction, faces an unpredictable regulatory environment which may impact project timelines and costs; delays in permits and clearances may lead to project overruns and increased liabilities. Management separately flags that despite proactive government support, infrastructure projects often face delays from complex regulatory clearances, land acquisition hurdles and environmental approvals, which increase project costs, reduce profitability and create uncertainty for private investors and EPC contractors.
- Dependence on government contracts and public funding — The sector's reliance on government contracts and funding makes the Company vulnerable to shifts in government priorities and budget allocations, affecting project continuity and profitability.
- Customer concentration on government authorities and receivables collection risk — The Company has a concentration of credit exposure on particular customers, being a government organisation, where there could be delays in collection for various reasons; management periodically assesses the adequacy of provisions on receivables and contract assets. Financial instruments subject to concentrations of credit risk principally consist of bank balances, investments in bonds, trade receivables and loans and advances.
- Raw material price volatility — Volatility in raw material prices such as steel and cement can increase construction costs and impact financial stability. The Company's key sourced inputs are fuel, cement, steel, aggregate and bitumen.
- Contract estimation and fixed-price execution risk — Revenue from construction contracts is recognised over time using the percentage-of-completion input method, so the major component of contract estimate is the budgeted cost to complete the contract. Contract prices are fixed in most cases, and due to technical complexities in the budgeting process contract estimates are highly sensitive to assumptions on execution manner, consumption norms and cost escalation. Estimation of total cost to complete involves significant judgement and requires provision for onerous contracts where applicable.
- Skilled labour shortages and technology/ESG compliance costs — Challenges include skilled labour shortages, the need for advanced technology and compliance with environmental, social and governance standards; these contribute to higher costs and operational complexities, requiring robust risk management and adaptive business models.
- Global economic and geopolitical uncertainty affecting inputs and financing — Fluctuating commodity prices, currency volatility and geopolitical tensions (for example in oil-producing regions or global shipping routes) can disrupt material supply chains and affect the financial performance of infrastructure projects that rely on imported equipment or raw materials. Elevated input costs and supply chain disruptions have had a pronounced impact on the infrastructure sector.
- Environmental and climate risk to construction schedules — The increasing frequency of extreme weather events, natural disasters and stricter ESG compliance expectations can disrupt construction schedules and impose additional costs; projects not aligned with sustainable development goals may face opposition from stakeholders and investors.
- Impairment risk on loans and investments extended to subsidiary SPVs — The Company has extended loans to subsidiaries and, due to the nature of infrastructure projects, is exposed to heightened risk in respect of impairment of loans granted to these related parties, with significant judgement and estimation uncertainty involved in assessing that impairment.
- Financial market risks - interest rate, liquidity and other price risk — The Company's financial risk framework identifies market risk (including interest rate risk and other price risk), credit risk and liquidity risk, with the Board assisted by a Risk Management Committee operating a Risk Management Policy covering identification, assessment, mitigation, reporting and review of critical risks.

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 marked Ceigall's decisive entry into renewable energy and power transmission, executed through the same Developer model of dedicated project SPVs that underpins its HAM road portfolio. The Company secured Letters of Award for a 220 MW solar plus BESS project from Rewa Ultra Mega Solar Ltd. in Madhya Pradesh (approximately Rs. 1,700 crore), multiple solar PV plants aggregating 130 MW under the PM KUSUM-C scheme with MP Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. (all 15 PPAs executed with MPPMCL at Rs. 2.85/unit), and a combined 337 MW of solar capacity in Maharashtra under MSKVY 2.0 through its subsidiaries Ceigall Green Energy MH1 and MH2 Limited (approximately Rs. 1,269 crore EPC value). It also entered power transmission and distribution through its acquisition of Velgaon Power Transmission Limited. A series of project SPVs were incorporated during the year to execute this pipeline: Ceigall Green Energy MH1 Limited (incorporated October 29, 2025) as solar power developer for an aggregate 190 MW(AC) under Mukhyamantri Saur Krushi Vahini Yojana 2.0, connected at 11 kV / 22 kV to MSEDCL / STU substations, contract value Rs. 7,313.80 million with the PPA signed March 24, 2026; Ceigall Green Energy MH2 Limited (incorporated October 29, 2025) on the same MSKVY 2.0 basis for an aggregate 147 MW(AC); Ceigall Green Energy MP Limited (incorporated January 05, 2026) for design, engineering, supply, construction, erection, testing and commissioning of grid-connected solar PV power plants of aggregate 190 MW(AC) under the Surya Mitra Krishi Feeders Scheme with the feeder solarisation component of PM KUSUM-C for sale of power to MPPMCL; and Ceigall Morena Solar Bess Park Limited (incorporated February 13, 2026) for a grid-connected ground-mounted solar PV project with Battery Energy Storage Systems at Morena Solar Park, Madhya Pradesh, including the 220 MW capacity awarded under the Rewa Ultra Mega Solar Limited tender, with a contract value of Rs. 14,875.40 million and the project under pipeline. A separate description of Ceigall Morena BESS Solar Park Limited covers development of a 600 MWAC grid-connected ground-mounted solar photovoltaic project with battery energy storage systems assuring 440 MW of peak power supply, to be set up in Morena Solar Park at Morena, Madhya Pradesh. On the roads side, Ceigall Indore Ujjain Greenfield Highway Limited was incorporated January 15, 2026 as an SPV of Ceigall India Limited along with wholly owned subsidiary Ceigall Infra Projects Private Limited, to develop and construct the Indore-Ujjain greenfield access-controlled 4-lane-with-paved-shoulder project highway of 48.10 km on Hybrid Annuity Mode in Madhya Pradesh awarded by Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation Limited, contract value Rs. 9,800.00 million with the concession agreement signed February 19, 2026 and preconstruction activities started. Ceigall Ambala Chandigarh Zirakpur Limited was incorporated April 28, 2026 as an SPV to construct a 6-lane access-controlled spur of 10.300 km from Ch. 15+100 of the Ambala-Chandigarh section of NH-205A to Ch. 2+500 of Zirakpur Bypass under NH(O) in Punjab on Hybrid Annuity Mode, contract value Rs. 5,500.00 million with the concession agreement signed 09 June 2026 and preconstruction activities started. On transmission, a project to plan, promote and develop an integrated power transmission system network - including transmission lines, sub-stations, load dispatch stations and communication facilities - carries a contract value of Rs. 4,067.80 million with the Transmission Service Agreement signed January 09, 2026, the entity having ceased to be a Government Company and become a Public Limited Company pursuant to a Share Purchase Agreement dated January 09, 2026. Two further balance-of-plant works remain under pipeline: Civil BOP works for the Aalla Projects at Rs. 1,507.20 million, and 220KV transmission line works for the Aalla Projects at Rs. 1,076.50 million. A further project with a contract value of Rs. 20,100.00 million has commenced preconstruction activities with the appointed date pending, and another of Rs. 1,430.00 million has its concession agreement signed with the appointed date pending. Alongside these additions the Company has initiated a structured capital recycling programme, monetising mature operational HAM assets - beginning with the divestment of its Malout-Abohar HAM asset - and redeploying proceeds into new project equity and balance sheet de-leveraging. Joint operations are conducted through unincorporated AOPs Ceigall IMC JV, Ceigall Shiva JV and Ceigall PEL JV, and a joint venture, RE Infra.

outlook.body:
- The Company aims to leverage the Indian government's focus on infrastructure development, which presents substantial opportunities across road construction, urban transit, clean energy and transmission infrastructure
- The Union Budget FY 2026-27 has a record capital expenditure outlay of INR 12.2 lakh crore, approximately 3.1% of GDP, with effective capital expenditure estimated at INR 15.48 lakh crore - continued investment expected to attract private capital, enhance productive capacity and structurally reduce logistics costs
- MoRTH capital expenditure was set at a record INR 3.10 lakh crore in the FY 2026-27 Budget Estimates, up from INR 2.87 lakh crore in the previous year
- Bharatmala Pariyojana remains the cornerstone of arterial road development; Phase I completion has been pushed to FY 2027-28 by land acquisition and clearance challenges, while Phase II preparatory work covering an additional 48,877 km is being integrated into the Vision 2047 infrastructure roadmap
- Adoption of PPP models such as the Hybrid Annuity Model has enhanced private sector participation and investor confidence in roads, metro rail, airports, ports, renewable energy and logistics
- Asset monetisation through InvITs and Toll-Operate-Transfer models has gained traction, enabling capital recycling and attracting institutional investment; NHAI realised INR 28,307 crore through asset monetisation in FY26
- Investment is increasingly directed toward renewable energy, power transmission and urban mobility alongside traditional transportation infrastructure
- Rapid urbanisation and rising incomes are fuelling demand for metro rail, urban expressways, multimodal transit hubs and smart mobility, especially in Tier II and Tier III cities where infrastructure gaps remain significant
- India's tunnelling infrastructure is expanding rapidly and the tunnel construction market is projected to grow at a double-digit CAGR, driven by demand across transport, urban transit and high-speed rail
- Indian GDP is expected to expand in the range of 6.8% to 7.2% in FY 2026-27, with economic activity supported by strong domestic demand and sustained government capital expenditure
- Elevated global energy prices, commodity price volatility and rupee depreciation have amplified input-cost pressures and pose challenges to infrastructure project economics
- As of FY 2025-26, the Company's order book is INR 1,85,543 million, spread across 97 ongoing projects - comprising 79 EPC, 10 HAM, 7 Tariff-Based (Renewable Energy) and 1 DBFOT project
- By value, HAM, Tariff-Based and DBFOT projects executed through the Developer model account for approximately 70% of the order book (HAM 48%, Tariff-Based 21%, DBFOT 1%), with the remaining 30% delivered through traditional EPC contracts
- As of March 2026 the order book stands at INR 18,554 crore, providing revenue visibility of approximately 4.8x of revenue
- As on March 31, 2026, the Company's total order book stood at approximately Rs. 1,85,543 million, providing strong revenue visibility for the coming years
- FY 2025-26 was driven by consistent execution across the core EPC business and robust order inflows in the highways and urban mobility sectors
- The Company has a strong, diversified order book spanning both its Developer and EPC models

risks.note: The Indian infrastructure sector, particularly highway, bridge and flyover construction, faces an unpredictable regulatory environment which may impact project timelines and costs; delays in permits and clearances may lead to project overruns and increased liabilities. Management separately flags that despite proactive government support, infrastructure projects often face delays from complex regulatory clearances, land acquisition hurdles and environmental approvals, which increase project costs, reduce profitability and create uncertainty for private investors and EPC contractors.

risks.risk: Dependence on government contracts and public funding
risks.note: The sector's reliance on government contracts and funding makes the Company vulnerable to shifts in government priorities and budget allocations, affecting project continuity and profitability.

risks.risk: Customer concentration on government authorities and receivables collection risk
risks.note: The Company has a concentration of credit exposure on particular customers, being a government organisation, where there could be delays in collection for various reasons; management periodically assesses the adequacy of provisions on receivables and contract assets. Financial instruments subject to concentrations of credit risk principally consist of bank balances, investments in bonds, trade receivables and loans and advances.

Volatility in raw material prices such as steel and cement can increase construction costs and impact financial stability. The Company's key sourced inputs are fuel, cement, steel, aggregate and bitumen.

risks.risk: Contract estimation and fixed-price execution risk
risks.note: Revenue from construction contracts is recognised over time using the percentage-of-completion input method, so the major component of contract estimate is the budgeted cost to complete the contract. Contract prices are fixed in most cases, and due to technical complexities in the budgeting process contract estimates are highly sensitive to assumptions on execution manner, consumption norms and cost escalation. Estimation of total cost to complete involves significant judgement and requires provision for onerous contracts where applicable.

risks.risk: Skilled labour shortages and technology/ESG compliance costs
risks.note: Challenges include skilled labour shortages, the need for advanced technology and compliance with environmental, social and governance standards; these contribute to higher costs and operational complexities, requiring robust risk management and adaptive business models.

risks.risk: Global economic and geopolitical uncertainty affecting inputs and financing
risks.note: Fluctuating commodity prices, currency volatility and geopolitical tensions (for example in oil-producing regions or global shipping routes) can disrupt material supply chains and affect the financial performance of infrastructure projects that rely on imported equipment or raw materials. Elevated input costs and supply chain disruptions have had a pronounced impact on the infrastructure sector.

risks.risk: Environmental and climate risk to construction schedules
risks.note: The increasing frequency of extreme weather events, natural disasters and stricter ESG compliance expectations can disrupt construction schedules and impose additional costs; projects not aligned with sustainable development goals may face opposition from stakeholders and investors.

risks.risk: Impairment risk on loans and investments extended to subsidiary SPVs
risks.note: The Company has extended loans to subsidiaries and, due to the nature of infrastructure projects, is exposed to heightened risk in respect of impairment of loans granted to these related parties, with significant judgement and estimation uncertainty involved in assessing that impairment.

risks.risk: Financial market risks - interest rate, liquidity and other price risk
risks.note: The Company's financial risk framework identifies market risk (including interest rate risk and other price risk), credit risk and liquidity risk, with the Board assisted by a Risk Management Committee operating a Risk Management Policy covering identification, assessment, mitigation, reporting and review of critical risks.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Ceigall India Limited is a construction company providing Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) services, specialising in highways, roads, tunnels, bridges and airport runways, and is also engaged in Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) projects across India through its subsidiaries. Alongside project-based EPC work it operates a Developer model of dedicated project SPVs backed by long-term Concession Agreements or Power Purchase Agreements, and in FY 2025-26 extended that model into solar photovoltaic generation with battery storage and into power transmission and distribution. It also undertakes Operation and Maintenance (O&M) agreements covering lighting, electrical systems, barriers, road maintenance and incident management, largely for government authority customers.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The Company aims to leverage the Indian government's focus on infrastructure development, which presents substantial opportunities across road construction, urban transit, clean energy and transmission infrastructure
- The Union Budget FY 2026-27 has a record capital expenditure outlay of INR 12.2 lakh crore, approximately 3.1% of GDP, with effective capital expenditure estimated at INR 15.48 lakh crore - continued investment expected to attract private capital, enhance productive capacity and structurally reduce logistics costs
- MoRTH capital expenditure was set at a record INR 3.10 lakh crore in the FY 2026-27 Budget Estimates, up from INR 2.87 lakh crore in the previous year
- Bharatmala Pariyojana remains the cornerstone of arterial road development; Phase I completion has been pushed to FY 2027-28 by land acquisition and clearance challenges, while Phase II preparatory work covering an additional 48,877 km is being integrated into the Vision 2047 infrastructure roadmap
- Adoption of PPP models such as the Hybrid Annuity Model has enhanced private sector participation and investor confidence in roads, metro rail, airports, ports, renewable energy and logistics
- Asset monetisation through InvITs and Toll-Operate-Transfer models has gained traction, enabling capital recycling and attracting institutional investment; NHAI realised INR 28,307 crore through asset monetisation in FY26
- Investment is increasingly directed toward renewable energy, power transmission and urban mobility alongside traditional transportation infrastructure
- Rapid urbanisation and rising incomes are fuelling demand for metro rail, urban expressways, multimodal transit hubs and smart mobility, especially in Tier II and Tier III cities where infrastructure gaps remain significant
- India's tunnelling infrastructure is expanding rapidly and the tunnel construction market is projected to grow at a double-digit CAGR, driven by demand across transport, urban transit and high-speed rail
- Indian GDP is expected to expand in the range of 6.8% to 7.2% in FY 2026-27, with economic activity supported by strong domestic demand and sustained government capital expenditure
- Elevated global energy prices, commodity price volatility and rupee depreciation have amplified input-cost pressures and pose challenges to infrastructure project economics
- As of FY 2025-26, the Company's order book is INR 1,85,543 million, spread across 97 ongoing projects - comprising 79 EPC, 10 HAM, 7 Tariff-Based (Renewable Energy) and 1 DBFOT project
- By value, HAM, Tariff-Based and DBFOT projects executed through the Developer model account for approximately 70% of the order book (HAM 48%, Tariff-Based 21%, DBFOT 1%), with the remaining 30% delivered through traditional EPC contracts
- As of March 2026 the order book stands at INR 18,554 crore, providing revenue visibility of approximately 4.8x of revenue
- As on March 31, 2026, the Company's total order book stood at approximately Rs. 1,85,543 million, providing strong revenue visibility for the coming years
- FY 2025-26 was driven by consistent execution across the core EPC business and robust order inflows in the highways and urban mobility sectors
- The Company has a strong, diversified order book spanning both its Developer and EPC models

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY 2025-26 marked Ceigall's decisive entry into renewable energy and power transmission, executed through the same Developer model of dedicated project SPVs that underpins its HAM road portfolio. The Company secured Letters of Award for a 220 MW solar plus BESS project from Rewa Ultra Mega Solar Ltd. in Madhya Pradesh (approximately Rs. 1,700 crore), multiple solar PV plants aggregating 130 MW under the PM KUSUM-C scheme with MP Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. (all 15 PPAs executed with MPPMCL at Rs. 2.85/unit), and a combined 337 MW of solar capacity in Maharashtra under MSKVY 2.0 through its subsidiaries Ceigall Green Energy MH1 and MH2 Limited (approximately Rs. 1,269 crore EPC value). It also entered power transmission and distribution through its acquisition of Velgaon Power Transmission Limited. A series of project SPVs were incorporated during the year to execute this pipeline: Ceigall Green Energy MH1 Limited (incorporated October 29, 2025) as solar power developer for an aggregate 190 MW(AC) under Mukhyamantri Saur Krushi Vahini Yojana 2.0, connected at 11 kV / 22 kV to MSEDCL / STU substations, contract value Rs. 7,313.80 million with the PPA signed March 24, 2026; Ceigall Green Energy MH2 Limited (incorporated October 29, 2025) on the same MSKVY 2.0 basis for an aggregate 147 MW(AC); Ceigall Green Energy MP Limited (incorporated January 05, 2026) for design, engineering, supply, construction, erection, testing and commissioning of grid-connected solar PV power plants of aggregate 190 MW(AC) under the Surya Mitra Krishi Feeders Scheme with the feeder solarisation component of PM KUSUM-C for sale of power to MPPMCL; and Ceigall Morena Solar Bess Park Limited (incorporated February 13, 2026) for a grid-connected ground-mounted solar PV project with Battery Energy Storage Systems at Morena Solar Park, Madhya Pradesh, including the 220 MW capacity awarded under the Rewa Ultra Mega Solar Limited tender, with a contract value of Rs. 14,875.40 million and the project under pipeline. A separate description of Ceigall Morena BESS Solar Park Limited covers development of a 600 MWAC grid-connected ground-mounted solar photovoltaic project with battery energy storage systems assuring 440 MW of peak power supply, to be set up in Morena Solar Park at Morena, Madhya Pradesh. On the roads side, Ceigall Indore Ujjain Greenfield Highway Limited was incorporated January 15, 2026 as an SPV of Ceigall India Limited along with wholly owned subsidiary Ceigall Infra Projects Private Limited, to develop and construct the Indore-Ujjain greenfield access-controlled 4-lane-with-paved-shoulder project highway of 48.10 km on Hybrid Annuity Mode in Madhya Pradesh awarded by Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation Limited, contract value Rs. 9,800.00 million with the concession agreement signed February 19, 2026 and preconstruction activities started. Ceigall Ambala Chandigarh Zirakpur Limited was incorporated April 28, 2026 as an SPV to construct a 6-lane access-controlled spur of 10.300 km from Ch. 15+100 of the Ambala-Chandigarh section of NH-205A to Ch. 2+500 of Zirakpur Bypass under NH(O) in Punjab on Hybrid Annuity Mode, contract value Rs. 5,500.00 million with the concession agreement signed 09 June 2026 and preconstruction activities started. On transmission, a project to plan, promote and develop an integrated power transmission system network - including transmission lines, sub-stations, load dispatch stations and communication facilities - carries a contract value of Rs. 4,067.80 million with the Transmission Service Agreement signed January 09, 2026, the entity having ceased to be a Government Company and become a Public Limited Company pursuant to a Share Purchase Agreement dated January 09, 2026. Two further balance-of-plant works remain under pipeline: Civil BOP works for the Aalla Projects at Rs. 1,507.20 million, and 220KV transmission line works for the Aalla Projects at Rs. 1,076.50 million. A further project with a contract value of Rs. 20,100.00 million has commenced preconstruction activities with the appointed date pending, and another of Rs. 1,430.00 million has its concession agreement signed with the appointed date pending. Alongside these additions the Company has initiated a structured capital recycling programme, monetising mature operational HAM assets - beginning with the divestment of its Malout-Abohar HAM asset - and redeploying proceeds into new project equity and balance sheet de-leveraging. Joint operations are conducted through unincorporated AOPs Ceigall IMC JV, Ceigall Shiva JV and Ceigall PEL JV, and a joint venture, RE Infra.

margins & cost dynamics: Guided EBITDA 11%-12.5% (conservative vs Q4's 14.1% standalone). Raw material inflation (iron ore) mitigated by monthly escalation clauses from authorities. Margins previously boosted by non-recurring bonus/royalty income; core operational margins stable.
capex / expansion: Equity investment requirement: INR 1,937 cr over next 3 years (INR 800 cr Renewable, rest HAM). Funding sources: HAM monetization proceeds (>INR 400 cr expected from NEO deal), internal accruals, unencumbered cash (INR 166 cr) and FDRs (INR 75 cr).
capital allocation: Priority on de-leveraging (D/E 0.2x standalone) and funding growth capex. HAM monetization proceeds to be deployed for both debt reduction and new project equity. Dividend policy not explicitly detailed but cash flow emphasized as robust.
risks & watch-items: Execution delay in BESS (Morena) pending land/PPA; Concentration risk in large single bids (Romania); Working capital strain (trade payables 138 days, unbilled revenue 133 days) though improving with monthly billing norms; International bid uncertainty (Romania result pending).
management quality / tone: Confident yet conservative; Emphasizes financial discipline, diversification success, and strong cash flows. Cautious on guidance (15% min) despite massive pipeline to manage expectations.
non-obvious takeaways: The INR 13,000 cr Romania bid is a single 17km highway project (vs ~INR 600-800 cr for similar length in India), highlighting massive international pricing arbitrage but also execution complexity. themes.title: Infrastructure EPC & roads order-book conversion
themes.need: India's record capital-outlay cycle (roads, metro, marine, hydro, tunnelling) gives diversified EPC contractors multi-year visibility - AFCONS tracks a ~INR4 lakh cr pipeline (70% domestic) and targets ~INR30,000cr FY27 inflow; NCC/DBL/PNCINFRA/GRINFRA/ASHOKA/CEIGALL carry large road/HAM books; AFCONS/PATELENG/AHLUCONT/PSPPROJECT add marine, hydro and building EPC. The binding issue is execution + client-payment cycles, not order intake.
themes.driver: L1-to-firm-order conversion (AFCONS Croatia/Vadhavan, DMRC awards); NHAI/HAM award pickup; monsoon-end execution ramp.

hero.oneLiner: Ceigall successfully pivoted from pure-play roads to a diversified energy-infrastructure mix, with renewables now comprising ~35% of FY26 inflows and a record order book of INR 18,554 cr. The strategic monetization of HAM assets via NEO Asset validates the 'build-monetize-recycle' model, freeing capital for aggressive growth in solar/BESS while maintaining a conservative 15% revenue guidance despite a 4.8x book-to-bill ratio.
